items.answer: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.

Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications use markers placed in the environment to trigger an augmented experience, and when a device detects a marker, the desired digital content appears at that marker's position in the real-world view.

The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.
The Microsoft HoloLens is one example of an augmented reality (AR) headset, and other such headsets are available.

questions.question: What is tracking in an extended reality system?
options: A type of virtual content
An integral hardware component
An optional software component
A form of immersive technology
questions.explanation: Tracking is described as an integral hardware component of an extended reality system.

questions.question: Keeping track of motion in the physical world is especially important in which XR area?
options: Augmented reality
Both virtual and augmented reality
Virtual reality
Mixed reality
questions.explanation: Tracking physical-world motion is crucial in any XR system, and it is more important in virtual reality systems.

questions.question: In virtual reality, what is tracking primarily used for?
options: Registering virtual content to a real-world anchor
Alerting the user to physical objects not represented in the virtual world
Translating the user's physical motion into virtual motion
Tracking only moving objects in the user's field of view
questions.explanation: In VR, tracking is primarily about tracking the user's physical motion or input so it can be translated into virtual motion.

questions.question: In augmented reality, what is tracking primarily about?
options: Translating the user's physical motion into virtual motion
Replacing the real environment with a virtual scene
Registering virtual content in 3D space with respect to a real-world anchor
Tracking only the user's head orientation
questions.explanation: In AR, tracking is primarily about registering virtual content in 3D space relative to a real-world anchor, while also tracking the user's pose and moving real-world objects.

data.text: Tracking is an integral hardware component of an XR system, and tracking motion in the physical world is crucial, more importantly in VR systems. In VR, tracking translates physical motion or input into virtual motion, while AR tracking registers virtual content in 3D space relative to a real-world anchor by tracking user pose and moving objects. Tracking is also called sensing, but the devices are more often called sensors than trackers.
points: Tracking is an integral hardware component of an XR system.
Tracking motion in the physical world is crucial, more importantly in VR systems.
In VR, tracking translates physical motion or input into virtual motion.
AR tracking registers virtual content in 3D space relative to a real-world anchor by tracking user pose and moving objects.
Tracking is also called sensing, but the devices are more often called sensors than trackers.

questions.question: What are the three categories of tracking based on what is being tracked?
options: Virtual reality, augmented reality, and telepresence
The user's sense organs, the user's other body parts, and the surrounding environment not related to the user
Outside-in tracking, inside-out tracking, and hybrid tracking
Head tracking, eye tracking, and hand tracking
questions.explanation: Tracking can be categorized by what is being tracked into tracking the user's sense organs, tracking the user's other body parts, and tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user.

questions.question: Why does an XR system need to track the position and orientation of the user's sense organs?
options: To capture live video of the physical world for telepresence
To register digital content to a real-world anchor
So a display attached to them can be perceived as attached to the surrounding world
To convert a button press into a predetermined virtual hand grasp
questions.explanation: Sense organs have body-controlled degrees of freedom, and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience.

questions.question: In VR, which sense-organ tracking is mostly sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears?
options: Facial expression tracking
Environmental object tracking
Head tracking
Eye tracking
questions.explanation: In VR, sense-organ tracking mostly focuses on head tracking, which is sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears.

questions.question: When is tracking of a user's other body parts required?
options: When a moved physical object must be registered in three-dimensional space
When the user needs to be alerted to a wall not represented in the virtual world
When the user wants a representation of the body in the virtual world, such as avatars or virtual hands
When live capture of the real world is added to the virtual world
questions.explanation: Tracking of the user's other body parts is required when the user wants a representation of the body in the virtual world, such as avatars or virtual hands, and gestures or facial expressions may be reproduced for interaction.

questions.question: In VR, why is tracking the surrounding environment useful for safety?
options: It can alert the user to physical objects not represented in the virtual world, such as a wall
It reproduces a user's hand gestures as virtual hands
It replaces head tracking for updating the virtual view
It registers digital content to a moved physical object
questions.explanation: In VR, tracking the surrounding environment can alert the user to physical objects not represented in the virtual world, such as a wall, helping to reduce harm.

data.text: Tracking in XR systems is categorized into sense organs, other body parts, and the surrounding environment. Sense organs are tracked so that displays are perceived as attached to the world, while other body parts can be tracked approximately or through simple input signals for virtual representations. Tracking the environment allows for the registration of digital content in AR and provides safety alerts or touch feedback in VR.
points: Tracking is categorized into sense organs, other body parts, and the surrounding environment.
Sense organs are tracked so that displays are perceived as attached to the world.
Other body parts can be tracked approximately or via explicit input signals for virtual representations.
Tracking the environment registers digital content in AR and provides safety alerts or touch feedback in VR.

questions.question: Which factors determine the choice of tracking method or technique?
options: Tracking process, user age, and headset weight
Tracker position, display resolution, and application domain
Tracker types, room size, and network latency
Tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types
questions.explanation: The choice of tracking depends on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types.

questions.question: Inside-out and outside-in tracking are categorized based on which feature?
options: The position of the tracker or sensor that provides input
The number of body parts being tracked
The type of display used for the experience
The domain in which the system is deployed
questions.explanation: Tracking is categorized into outside-in and inside-out based on the position of the tracker or sensor that provides input.

questions.question: In outside-in tracking, where are the tracking sensors located?
options: In the experience device worn by the user
In external sensors or trackers in the real world
In the virtual world shown to the user
In the user's eyes only, using eye tracking
questions.explanation: In outside-in tracking, the experience device does not contain the tracking sensors; external real-world sensors or trackers provide the data.

questions.question: Why can inside-out tracking avoid the area restriction of outside-in tracking?
options: It uses a higher-resolution head-mounted display
It tracks only virtual objects in the environment
Its tracking sensors are worn by or attached to the user
It removes the need for any user motion data
questions.explanation: Outside-in tracking works only within the range of its external sensors, while inside-out tracking avoids that restriction because the sensors are worn or attached to the user.

questions.question: Which tracking category includes most VR headsets that use external sensors?
options: Body-part tracking
Environment tracking
Outside-in tracking
Inside-out tracking
questions.explanation: Most VR headsets that use external sensors are described as falling under outside-in tracking.

data.text: The choice of tracking depends on tracker position, process, and types, and is categorized as outside-in or inside-out. Outside-in tracking uses external sensors but is limited to a specific area. Inside-out tracking uses sensors within the device and has no such restriction.
points: The choice of tracking method depends on tracker position, process, and types.
Tracking is categorized as outside-in or inside-out based on sensor position.
Outside-in tracking uses external sensors but is limited to a specific area.
Inside-out tracking uses sensors within the device and has no such restriction.

questions.question: What are the four broad steps of the tracking process?
options: Calibration, registration, integration, and pose correction
Calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction
Calibration, localization, integration, and drift correction
Calibration, registration, interpolation, and drift correction
questions.explanation: The tracking process broadly consists of calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.

questions.question: In tracking, what does calibration primarily do?
options: Transforms imperfect sensor output toward the real value, reducing sensor error
Compensates for differences between estimated and actual position and orientation
Estimates the sensor's initial position and orientation, setting the start point
Aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors at discrete time points
questions.explanation: Calibration is the step that transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error.

questions.question: In tracking, what is the purpose of registration?
options: Compensates for differences between estimated and actual position and orientation
Determines the sensor's initial position and orientation before movement is tracked
Transforms imperfect sensor output toward the real value, reducing sensor error
Aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors at discrete time points
questions.explanation: Registration estimates or determines the initial position and orientation of the sensor, so that the starting point is known before movement can be tracked.

questions.question: In tracking, what does integration do?
options: Transforms imperfect sensor output toward the real value, reducing sensor error
Aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or data sources at discrete time points
Compensates for differences between estimated and actual position and orientation
Determines the sensor's initial position and orientation before movement is tracked
questions.explanation: Integration aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment.

questions.question: In tracking, what does drift correction do?
options: Transforms imperfect sensor output toward the real value, reducing sensor error
Determines the sensor's initial position and orientation before movement is tracked
Compensates for differences between estimated and actual position and orientation, reducing estimation error
Aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or data sources at discrete time points
questions.explanation: Drift correction compensates for the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation of the user, the user's sense organs, body parts, or objects in the environment, reducing estimation error.

data.text: Tracking input can be obtained via inside-out or outside-in methods. The tracking process consists of calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction. Calibration transforms sensor output to behave as closely as possible to natural values, while registration determines the initial position and orientation. Integration combines measurements from multiple sources, and drift correction compensates for differences between estimated and actual positions to reduce error.
points: Tracking input can be obtained using inside-out or outside-in methods.
The tracking process consists of calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.
Calibration transforms sensor output to behave as closely as possible to natural values.
Registration determines the initial position and orientation of the sensor.
Integration combines measurements from multiple sources, while drift correction compensates for differences between estimated and actual positions.

questions.question: How do pose estimation and environment tracking together support the registration of digital content in augmented reality?
questions.reference_answer: Augmented reality is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content. To register virtual content in augmented reality, the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, because without proper pose estimation three-dimensional registration is difficult or impossible. In augmented reality, tracking also requires moving real-world objects in the field of view, and a moved physical object must be tracked in the real-world view so that digital content can be appropriately registered. Environment tracking is more important in augmented reality for this purpose, although it is also important in virtual reality.

questions.question: How does the position of a sensor determine the two broad ways to obtain tracking input, and why does that affect where outside-in tracking can work?
questions.reference_answer: Tracking is categorized based on the position of the tracker or sensor into outside-in and inside-out tracking. In outside-in tracking, the experience device does not contain the sensors; external sensors such as cameras or markers provide data to identify and track motion, pose, and orientation. Outside-in tracking works only within the sensor range where those external sensors are placed. Inside-out tracking locates cameras or other sensors within the experience device, such as a head-mounted display, so no external devices are needed and there is no such placement restriction.

questions.question: What different errors are reduced by calibration and drift correction in the tracking process?
questions.reference_answer: The tracking process broadly consists of calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction. Calibration transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error. Drift correction compensates for the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation, reducing estimation error.

questions.question: How does sense-organ tracking support a display attached to a user's sense organ, and when might eye tracking be added to head tracking in virtual reality?
questions.reference_answer: Sense organs such as eyes and ears have body-controlled degrees of freedom, and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience. In virtual reality, sense-organ tracking mostly focuses on head tracking, which is sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears. Eye tracking may be required if rendering and display technology require compensating for eye movement, and eye tracking may be part of head tracking.
